tier_reason: README 'Benchmarks' section scenario 3 shows the exact sizes (Protobuf 3,108,000 bytes vs JSBT 64,175 bytes, '48x smaller than Protobuf'), but methodology is only 'run on Node.js', no CPU/Node version, and the public harness benchmarks/benchmark1.ts only runs JSON and JSBT, so the Protobuf/MsgPack/CBOR rows are not reproducible from published code: first-party, partial methodology = C.

corrections.caveats: Author states the benchmarks are 'synthetic and indicative, not absolute' and were 'run on Node.js'; no hardware, Node version, or Protobuf library/schema details given. The public benchmark harness (benchmarks/benchmark1.ts) only compares JSON vs JSBT; the Protobuf, MsgPack and CBOR rows in the README tables have no published harness. The repeated dataset is built to favor deduplication (id i%100, name i%50, one shared scores array, identical tags/meta), and sizes are uncompressed (no gzip/zstd comparison). The win is compactness only, not speed: on the README's simple-flat-object table JSBT encode is 31.51 us/op vs Protobuf 3.29 us/op and decode 20.83 vs 1.95 us/op (roughly 10x slower); the repeated-data table gives timings for JSBT only (encode ~1,029 ms/op, decode ~43 ms/op), not for Protobuf. README is slightly inconsistent on the JSBT size (64,175 bytes / 62.7 KB in the table vs '~60.5 kb' in the text below it).

notes: Numbers and repo metadata (MIT, 36 stars, not fork/archived, last commit 2026-04-05, active) all check out. Only the caveats needed tightening: the earlier claim that JSBT is slower than Protobuf 'on the same tables' holds only for the simple-object table, and the Protobuf comparison code is not public.

tier_reason: Table 10 of arXiv 1902.08318 (identical in v4-v7; VLDB Journal 2019) reports cJSON and nlohmann/json ('JSON for Modern C++') GB/s on 14 files with GCC 9.1 -O3 -march=native on an Intel i7-6700 Skylake, and footnote 4 publishes the code: github.com/simdjson/simdjson_experiments_vldb2019 experiments/comparison (Dockerfile FROM gcc:9.1, build.sh/run.sh) driving benchmark/parsingcompetition.cpp and allparsingcompetition in the pinned lemire/simdjson submodule, so tier A stands; the verdict is downgrade only because the claim misquotes the baseline numbers and overstates 'all 14'.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 10 (Skylake, GB/s): cJSON is faster than nlohmann/json ('JSON for Modern C++') on 13 of 14 files and ties on mesh (0.06 vs 0.06 GB/s), e.g. gsoc-2018 0.53 vs 0.12 GB/s (~4.4x), twitter 0.33 vs 0.10 (~3.3x), citm_catalog 0.36 vs 0.14 (~2.6x); on number-heavy files the margin is small (canada 0.07 vs 0.05, marine_ik 0.07 vs 0.06, numbers 0.07 vs 0.06, mesh.pretty 0.13 vs 0.11) (derived from page data). cJSON also beats jsoncpp on all 14 files and jsmn on 11 of 14, losing github_events (0.28 vs 0.52), marine_ik (0.07 vs 0.18) and numbers (0.07 vs 0.65) (derived from page data). RapidJSON (default mode) beats cJSON on 13 of 14 files; cJSON is ahead only on gsoc-2018 (0.53 vs 0.51 GB/s); RapidJSON insitu beats cJSON on all 14 (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Earlier versions of this record misread Table 10: nlohmann/json is 0.12 GB/s on gsoc-2018 (not 0.14) and 0.06 on mesh (a tie with cJSON, not 0.05), and cJSON beats jsmn on 11 of 14 files, so the seed lead's '11 of 14' was correct. cJSON only wins against RapidJSON on 1 of 14 files (gsoc-2018, 0.53 vs 0.51, a 4% gap), so nlohmann/json (13 wins, 1 tie) is the honest baseline for a 'beats' claim, not RapidJSON. Table 10 gives only two significant digits, so the number-heavy files (canada, marine_ik, mesh, mesh.pretty, numbers; margins 0-0.02 GB/s) are near-ties. Numbers are from 2019 ('latest available version' of each parser, cJSON version not stated); the artifact repo's March 2020 Skylake rerun (results/skylake/comparison, not the paper) has nlohmann slightly ahead on mesh (0.066 vs 0.061 GB/s) while cJSON still leads on the other 13 files. All libraries have changed many times since, so the gap may be different today. nativejson-benchmark (https://github.com/miloyip/nativejson-benchmark) lists cJSON 1.5.0 among its tested libraries, which supports cJSON being a recognized shootout entrant, but its per-library numbers were not extracted and it is cited only as corroboration.

notes: The tier (A) and the metadata (MIT, 13,011 stars, last commit 2026-09-16, active, not fork/archived) are correct. The verdict is downgrade because the claim was wrong, not the tier: the record quoted wrong nlohmann numbers (gsoc 0.14 should be 0.12; mesh 0.05 should be 0.06, a tie), overstated 'all 14' (it is 13 wins plus a tie), and wrongly said the jsmn count was 10/14 when it is 11/14. The artifact repo's 2019-06 raw results for cJSON, jsmn and RapidJSON match Table 10; nlohmann raw numbers for Table 10 were not in those 2019 files.
